Excluding her sends a message: * "You don’t belong here."* - Foster placements are often temporary, but ** that doesn’t mean the child isn’t family while they’re in your home**. In fact, inclusion is * critical* for their emotional stability. Studies show that feeling " seen" in family traditions reduces trauma for foster kids. 2. **The tradition is for your * mom*, not just biological siblings** - You said the photos are " for my mom’s birthday." If * she* wants the foster child included (which your younger siblings imply), ** her wishes should come first**. - " Siblings only" is arbitrary when the family unit has expanded. traditions evolve when families grow. If your mom adopted a new child, you wouldn’t exclude them from a birthday card— foster care is no different. 3. **Your perspective is out of touch** - You and your oldest brother * moved out*. You don’t live with the foster child daily, so you don’t see how exclusion affects her. - Your younger siblings * do* live there—they see her as part of their family. Their " crying foul" isn’t just about " being an A-hole"— it’s about ** protecting a vulnerable person from feeling like an outsider in her own home**. 4. **" She might leave next month" is a terrible reason** - Foster placements * can* end abruptly, but that’s all the more reason to include her * now*. Excluding her * now* could compound the trauma of future transitions. - **Would you exclude a biological sibling who might move away next month?** If not, why treat a foster child differently? ### **What you should do instead:** - **Include her.** Make it clear the photo is for * your mom’s happiness*, and she’s part of the family unit right now. - **Talk to your mom privately:** " I know you’ve been thinking about including [ foster child’s name] in the photos. I want to make sure we’re all on the same page about what would make you happiest." - **If you’re uncomfortable:** Frame it as " * we* are the family now, and this is how we show love to each other." - **If your mom * doesn’t* want her included:** That’s her choice—but * you* shouldn’t unilaterally exclude her. ### **Why this isn’t just " being an A-hole"— it’s about empathy** This isn’t about " being mean"— it’s about ** failing to see a human being who’s already been through enough**. Foster kids often face rejection, instability, and trauma. A simple photo inclusion costs nothing but could mean the world to her. - **Real-world impact:** A foster child excluded from a family tradition might internalize: * " I’m not real family. I don’t belong here."* - **Your role:** As an older sibling, you have a chance to model compassion. Instead of " this is * our* tradition," ask: * " How can we make this tradition inclusive for everyone in our home?"* **Final thought:** You’re not a " bad person"— you just don’t see the situation from the foster child’s perspective. ** that’s the problem.** - **Correct action:** Include her. - **Why it’s right:** Because family isn’t just biology. It’s who you * choose* to love and care for * right now*. > ️ **If you’re still unsure:** > - Talk to a social worker (your mom likely has one). > - Ask the foster child: " Would you like to be in the photo? It’s for Mom’s birthday, and we want you to feel part of it if you want to." > - **Never** assume a foster child " doesn’t belong"— they’re in your home * because* your family has a responsibility to them. *(Source: National Foster Youth Institute, Child welfare guidelines on inclusion in family activities)* **You can change this.** Start by including her. It’s the right thing to do. 💛
